children.text: Understanding what
spinal injury compensation

may cover is one of the most important steps after a life-changing accident. These cases are rarely straightforward. The physical recovery alone can take months or years, while the financial toll of ongoing medical treatment, rehabilitation, and lifestyle adjustments can feel overwhelming. At
Dormer Harpring
, we’ve worked with Coloradans whose spinal injuries have altered every part of their daily lives—and we know the numbers behind a fair recovery must reflect that reality.
Understanding the Impact of Spinal Injuries
Spinal cord injuries

reach far beyond the initial trauma. They often cause lasting changes in mobility, sensation, and organ function, along with chronic pain, emotional distress, and loss of independence. A spinal cord injury affects not only the person hurt but also their family’s finances, relationships, and long-term planning.
A
spinal cord injury

can damage the spinal cord itself or the nerves at its base, known as the cauda equina. Because the spinal cord controls the signals between the brain and the body, this type of injury can cause permanent changes below the site of impact—altering strength, sensation, and other essential functions.
Types of Spinal Cord Injuries
Incomplete Spine Injury

An incomplete injury means the spinal cord still transmits some signals below the affected area. Victims may retain limited movement or sensation. The degree of impairment varies widely—from mild weakness to significant paralysis. Because the outcome can improve with early intervention, the cost of rehabilitation, therapy, and assistive technology plays a critical role in case valuation.
Complete Spine Injury

A complete injury cuts off all sensory and motor function below the injury site. Paralysis may occur on both sides of the body, often classified as paraplegia or quadriplegia. These cases typically involve lifelong personal care, specialized medical equipment, and extensive home modification, which significantly influence the total compensation a person may recover.
Levels of Spinal Injuries
Medical professionals classify spinal cord injuries by their location along the spine:
Cervical (neck area)
– Usually the most severe; can cause full or partial paralysis in arms, legs, and torso.
Thoracic (upper and mid-back)
– May result in loss of movement or sensation in the lower body while preserving arm function.
Lumbar and sacral (lower back)
– Often impact leg movement, bladder control, and sexual function.
Each level affects daily life differently, and compensation calculations must reflect the distinct medical and lifestyle consequences that come with each classification.
Categories of Compensation in Spinal Injury Cases
A spinal injury claim covers both tangible and intangible losses. Our role is to ensure every category is identified, proven, and valued correctly.
Medical Expenses

Immediate and future medical costs form the foundation of any spinal injury claim. These include emergency treatment, surgeries, hospitalization, rehabilitation, medication, and ongoing physical or occupational therapy. Projected future expenses, such as maintenance of medical devices or attendant care, must also be included.
Lost Income
When an injury prevents a person from working temporarily, the lost wages should be reimbursed. This figure is verified through employment records, tax documents, and medical restrictions.
Loss of Earning Capacity

When a spinal cord injury permanently limits the ability to return to a previous job or earn at the same level, Colorado law allows compensation for loss of earning capacity. Vocational experts and economists often testify to calculate the lifetime difference between expected and diminished earnings.
Pain and Suffering

Colorado recognizes that no financial figure can truly capture the physical pain or emotional distress caused by a spinal cord injury. However, state law places limits on these non-economic damages. Under
Colorado Revised Statutes (C.R.S.) § 13-21-102.5
, known as Limitations on Damages for Noneconomic Loss or Injury, awards are capped to protect the public welfare while still ensuring fair recovery.
Home and Vehicle Modifications

Serious spinal injuries often require remodeling a home for wheelchair access, installing ramps, widening doorways, or converting bathrooms and vehicles. These costs are recoverable and must be supported by contractor estimates or reports from accessibility experts.
Long-Term or Lifetime Care Costs

When independence is reduced, in-home caregivers or assisted-living arrangements may be necessary. These costs—often extending over decades—should be projected through medical life care planning and economic analysis. The goal is to ensure lifelong dignity and stability.
How Is Spinal Injury Compensation Calculated?
Valuing a claim for
spinal injury compensation
involves both economic and non-economic factors. While no universal formula exists, several consistent elements influence outcomes:
Severity and permanence of the injury.
Courts and insurers assess medical records, imaging, and testimony from treating physicians.
Total economic impact.
This includes current bills, expected medical care, and long-term rehabilitation costs.
Effect on work and daily life.
How the injury limits employment, hobbies, and relationships often guides non-economic valuations.
Comparative negligence.

Under Colorado’s modified comparative negligence law, defined in C.R.S. §13-21-111, an injured person may still recover damages if their own negligence was not as great as the other party’s. However, the total recovery is reduced in proportion to the percentage of fault assigned to them.
Insurance coverage and policy limits.
The available coverage can influence settlement negotiations, particularly in catastrophic injury cases.

Why Legal Representation Matters in Spinal Injury Claims
The process of seeking
spinal injury compensation

can feel daunting. Insurance companies may offer early settlements that barely address immediate expenses, ignoring the long-term costs of care and lost independence. An experienced legal team can uncover every available source of recovery—from liability insurance to underinsured-motorist coverage, workers’ compensation, and third-party claims.

Our approach is built on preparation and transparency. We start by gathering every record, bill, and expert opinion necessary to quantify future needs. We also handle insurer communication and negotiate from a position of documented strength, backed by our results in catastrophic injury cases throughout Colorado.

Because each client’s story is unique, we avoid generic formulas. Instead, we use individualized evidence to demonstrate the daily realities of living with a spinal injury, the moments insurance adjusters never see, and how those realities justify full compensation under Colorado law.
